title: Najd on the Eve of the Reform
subtitle: 1517–1744 · The Oasis-Town Emirates, Banū Khālid Overlordship and the Road to the Pact of Dirʿiyya

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Two centuries of feuding oasis-town emirates under a distant Banū Khālid overlordship, and the arrival of the reformer whose expulsion from al-ʿUyayna sent him to Dirʿiyya

entries.label: The oasis-town emirates
entries.loc: Wadi Ḥanīfa, al-Qaṣīm and Sudayr, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Najd stayed a patchwork of walled towns, each under an amīr from a leading family — the Muʿammar at al-ʿUyayna, the Āl Saʿūd at Dirʿiyya, the amīrs of Riyadh, Manfūḥa, Ḥuraymilāʾ, al-Majmaʿa, Buraydah and ʿUnayzah — none strong, all at feud.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd; Uwaidah al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002).

entries.label: The Āl Saʿūd of Dirʿiyya
entries.hint: From Māniʿ al-Muraydī's settlement the family grew from holding one quarter of Dirʿiyya to holding the whole town — small amīrs among many, by the early 18th century under Saʿūd ibn Muḥammad and then Muḥammad ibn Saʿūd.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the Dirʿiyya dynastic tradition; Madawi Al-Rasheed, 'A History of Saudi Arabia' (2010).

entries.label: The Muʿammar of al-ʿUyayna
entries.hint: Al-ʿUyayna was for a time the strongest town of the district under the Āl Muʿammar. Its amīr ʿUthmān ibn Muʿammar first backed Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb and then, under Banū Khālid pressure, expelled him.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar; Ibn Bishr; al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: Banū Khālid overlordship
entries.hint: The Banū Khālid, having taken al-Aḥsāʾ from the Ottomans around 1670, made themselves the dominant power of eastern Arabia under the Āl Ḥumayd — Barrāk ibn Ghurayr, then Saʿdūn — and extended a loose, tribute-collecting suzerainty over much of Najd.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the Ottoman and Portuguese records of eastern Arabia; al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: The Ottoman and Sharifian fringe
entries.loc: the Hijaz and al-Aḥsāʾ · claiming the Najd margins
entries.hint: The Ottomans held the Hijaz and, intermittently, al-Aḥsāʾ, but never Najd. The sharifs of Mecca claimed the Najd–Hijaz borderland and the Hajj routes and raided into the interior from time to time — the outer edge of an empire that never came in.
entries.note: Hathaway, 'The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule' (2008); the sharifian chronicles of Mecca.

entries.group: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb and the Road to Dirʿiyya (1703–1744)
entries.label: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, the early years
entries.hint: Born at al-ʿUyayna into a scholarly Ḥanbalī family, he studied in Medina and Basra — where his preaching against shrine practice got him expelled — and returned to Ḥuraymilāʾ, where his father was qāḍī, to write the Kitāb al-Tawḥīd.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar; Michael Cook, 'On the Origins of Wahhābism' (1992); Natana DeLong-Bas, 'Wahhabi Islam' (2004).

entries.group: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb and the Road to Dirʿiyya (1703–1744)
entries.label: The al-ʿUyayna experiment and the expulsion
entries.hint: After his father's death he moved to al-ʿUyayna, won over its amīr, and enforced his doctrine — felling sacred trees, demolishing the tomb of Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ordering a stoning. The Banū Khālid amīr of al-Aḥsāʾ threatened Ibn Muʿammar, who expelled him.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām; Ibn Bishr; Cook (1992).

entries.group: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb and the Road to Dirʿiyya (1703–1744)
entries.label: The pact of Dirʿiyya
entries.hint: Expelled from al-ʿUyayna, Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb was received at Dirʿiyya by its amīr Muḥammad ibn Saʿūd. The two swore a mutual oath — the amīr to protect and spread the doctrine, the shaykh to back the amīr's authority. It is the founding compact of the Saudi state.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām; Ibn Bishr; the mubāyaʿa is reconstructed from the Wahhābī chronicles. Traditionally dated 1744 (1157 AH).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The endemic small war of the town emirates, Banū Khālid punitive marches, the bedouin pressure on the settled districts, and the first acts of Wahhābī enforcement

entries.label: The wars of the town emirates
entries.hint: Chronic small-scale war between the towns and their tribal allies — raids on palm groves, sieges of a few weeks, coalitions that formed and broke each season. It is the disorder the Wahhābī chroniclers would later call a return to jāhiliyya.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd, whose annals are largely a list of these campaigns; al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: Banū Khālid marches into Najd
entries.hint: The Āl Ḥumayd repeatedly led their tribes into the plateau to punish a town, install an amīr or collect an overdue tribute — the main external violence in Najd, and the mechanism by which they kept any one Najdi power from rising.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: The bedouin pressure and the bad years
entries.hint: ʿUtayba, Muṭayr, Qaḥṭān, Shammar and ʿAnaza pressed hard on the oasis districts, and a year that combined raiding with drought could empty a town. The chronicles reckon history in good and bad years as much as in reigns.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the poetry of Ḥmēdān al-Shwēʿir on the failed harvests and the raids.

entries.label: The first acts of enforcement
entries.hint: Felling the venerated trees, demolishing the tomb at al-Jubayla and carrying out a stoning were acts of religious violence against the existing order. They made Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb too dangerous for a small-town amīr under Banū Khālid pressure to keep.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar; Cook (1992).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The town amirate and its council, the extractive lightness of Banū Khālid rule, and the 1744 oath that divided temporal from religious authority

entries.label: The town amirate and the majlis
entries.hint: Each town was run by its amīr through a council of the leading heads of family, with a qāḍī applying Ḥanbalī law and a militia of the townsmen. It was a workable local government — and it had no reach beyond the town wall.
entries.note: al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002); Ibn Bishr.

entries.label: Banū Khālid tribute and arbitration
entries.hint: The Āl Ḥumayd's suzerainty ran as tribute demands and as arbitration of the towns' quarrels — a light, extractive overlordship whose whole purpose was to stop any Najdi power from rising. That is exactly why they moved against Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: The oath of 1744
entries.hint: The mubāyaʿa at Dirʿiyya was a constitutional act: it defined a division of authority between a temporal ruler, the Āl Saʿūd, and a religious authority, the Āl al-Shaykh and the ʿulamāʾ, that has structured the Saudi state through all three of its foundations.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām; the analysis in Guido Steinberg, 'Religion und Staat in Saudi-Arabien' (2002).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The folk religion of the oases, the Ḥanbalī hadith revival of Medina, the doctrine of tawḥīd, and the first Sunni refutations of it

entries.label: The religion the reform attacked
entries.hint: Tombs, trees, caves and stones across Najd received vows and offerings — Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb at al-Jubayla, the 'male palm' of Dhū Saʿab, the cave of Bint al-Amīr, the tomb of Ḍirār. This is the practice Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb defined as shirk, associating others with God.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar (listing the sites the movement destroyed); al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: The Medina hadith revival
entries.hint: In the Ḥaramayn a circle of scholars — Ibrāhīm al-Kūrānī's successors, Muḥammad Ḥayāt al-Sindī, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Sayf — pressed a return to hadith and to Ibn Taymiyya. Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb studied with them and took the method home.
entries.note: John Voll, 'Muḥammad Ḥayyā al-Sindī and Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb'; Cook (1992).
keywords: Abd Allāh ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Sayf

entries.label: The doctrine of tawḥīd
entries.hint: Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's core claim: the profession of God's oneness requires that every act of worship, vow, sacrifice and appeal be directed to God alone, and that seeking intercession at a tomb or a tree is idolatry that puts the person outside Islam.
entries.note: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, Kitāb al-Tawḥīd and Kashf al-Shubuhāt; DeLong-Bas, 'Wahhabi Islam' (2004).

entries.label: The first refutations
entries.hint: Najdi ʿulamāʾ, in the tradition his own brother Sulaymān among them, argued that the movement's charge of unbelief against ordinary Muslims was itself the error of the Kharijites. The internal Sunni argument over Wahhābism began at once and has never stopped.
entries.note: Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, al-Ṣawāʿiq al-ilāhiyya (attribution and date debated); Cook (1992); Samer Traboulsi on the early refutations.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The mature earthen town and its painted majlis, the great satirist Ḥmēdān al-Shwēʿir, the amīr-poets who corresponded in verse, and the samir and the ʿarda

entries.label: The mature Najdi town and the majlis style
entries.hint: At-Turaif at Dirʿiyya, old ʿUnayzah and Ushayqir show the developed earthen architecture — the qaṣr, the columned majlis with its triangular wall-niches and incised white plaster, the mosque with its ramp minaret — the 'Najdi style' in its classic form.
entries.note: Geoffrey King, 'The Traditional Architecture of Saudi Arabia' (1998); the at-Turaif quarter of Dirʿiyya, a UNESCO World Heritage site (2010).

entries.label: Ḥmēdān al-Shwēʿir
entries.hint: Ḥumaydān al-Shuwayʿir of al-Qaṣab was the outstanding Nabaṭī poet of pre-Saudi Najd — a satirist and moralist whose gnomic verse is a bitter, first-hand witness to the poverty, the feuding and the failure of the amīrs.
entries.note: the dīwān of Ḥmēdān al-Shwēʿir; Saad Sowayan, 'Nabaṭi Poetry' (1985); P. Marcel Kurpershoek's editions and translations.

entries.label: The amīr-poets
entries.loc: al-Ghāṭ, Sudayr and the Wadi Ḥanīfa towns
entries.hint: Rumayzān ibn Ghashshām of al-Ghāṭ, Jaʿaythin al-Yazīdī and other town rulers exchanged formal poems of challenge, alliance and lament. In a land with no chancery, Nabaṭī verse was the diplomatic correspondence of the emirates.
entries.note: Kurpershoek, 'Oral Poetry and Narratives from Central Arabia'; the corpus of the early Nabaṭī amīr-poets.

entries.label: The samir, the ʿarda and the women's song
entries.hint: The night poetry-gathering (samir), the sword-dance of the town militia (ʿarda), and the women's wedding and work songs made up the performance life that ran on under the political chaos and that the reform movement would later view with suspicion.
entries.note: Sowayan on the samir; Lisa Urkevich, 'Music and Traditions of the Arabian Peninsula' (2015).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The plain teaching texts of the reform, the raw town annals that would become the first Najdi histories, and the transmitted authority of Ibn Taymiyya

entries.label: Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's writings
entries.hint: The Kitāb al-Tawḥīd, the Kashf al-Shubuhāt and the Thalāthat al-Uṣūl — short, plain, hadith-anchored texts written to teach a semi-literate society. They are still the core curriculum of the tradition he founded, in Saudi Arabia and far beyond.
entries.note: the collected works (Muʾallafāt al-Shaykh); DeLong-Bas, 'Wahhabi Islam' (2004).

entries.label: The Najdi town annals
entries.hint: The anonymous town chronicles and family records of 17th–18th-century Najd — dry lists of amīrs, raids, harvests and prices — are the raw material Ibn Ghannām and Ibn Bishr later worked into the first true histories of the plateau.
entries.note: the Najdi akhbar tradition; ʿAbd Allah al-ʿUthaymin on the sources for early Najdi history.

entries.label: The transmission of Ibn Taymiyya
entries.loc: Ushayqir and the Najdi scholarly towns
entries.hint: The works of the 14th-century Damascus jurist, copied and taught in the Najdi towns since the late medieval period, gave Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb his authorities and his method. The reform was a Najdi application of an older Ḥanbalī argument, not a new one.
entries.note: Cook, 'On the Origins of Wahhābism' (1992); the Najdi manuscript record of Ibn Taymiyya's works.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Dates paying tribute to the desert, the Qaṣīmi merchant caravans and the global trade in the Najdi horse, and an economy that a run of dry years could break

entries.label: The date-and-khuwa economy
entries.hint: The towns lived on the date palm and paid a share of the crop as protection tribute to the dominant tribe or to Banū Khālid. The settled economy was productive but exposed — a hostage to the desert around it.
entries.note: al-Juhany (2002); Ibn Bishr on the tribute demands.

entries.label: The ʿUqaylāt and the horse trade
entries.loc: al-Qaṣīm · to Iraq, Syria, Egypt and India
entries.hint: Najdi merchants — the ʿUqaylāt, mostly from al-Qaṣīm — drove caravans of camels and horses to Iraq, Syria and Egypt, and the trade in the Najdi mare to India through the Gulf ports made her a global luxury and a serious source of tribal and town wealth.
entries.note: the accounts of the ʿUqaylāt trade (Musil; the later travel literature); the Indian and Egyptian demand for the Najdi horse.

entries.label: The pastoral economy and the tribes
entries.hint: Camel and small-stock herding, the exchange of animals and transport labour with the towns, and the raid — the same structure as the medieval centuries, and no richer. The plateau's poverty is the constant of this folio.
entries.note: al-Juhany (2002); the ethnographic literature on Najdi pastoralism.

entries.label: Drought, famine and the fragile town
entries.hint: A run of dry years or a single lost harvest could break a town's economy and its politics at once. The Najdi chronicles measure time in years of plenty and years of hunger — sanat al-jūʿ, the year of the famine — as much as in the reigns of amīrs.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the famine years recorded in the Najdi annals; the poetry of Ḥmēdān al-Shwēʿir.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Well irrigation at the ceiling of what a town could water, and firearms arriving slowly and expensively on the plateau

entries.label: Well irrigation at its limit
entries.hint: The deep well and the animal-drawn bucket had reached the practical ceiling of what a Najdi town could water. Town size, and so town power, was capped by the depth of the water table and the number of wells a family could dig and man.
entries.note: King, 'The Traditional Architecture of Saudi Arabia' (1998); al-Juhany (2002) on the demographic ceiling.

entries.label: Firearms reach the plateau
entries.hint: The matchlock and then the flintlock spread slowly into Najd through the Gulf and Hijaz trade, changing the town siege and the raid. But powder and shot were scarce and dear, and the sword and the lance still decided most fights.
entries.note: the arms references in Ibn Bishr; the wider history of firearms in Arabia.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Study in the Ḥaramayn, a first clash with an urban Muslim society at Basra, the al-Aḥsāʾ connection that sent the shaykh to Dirʿiyya, and the Qaṣīmi merchant diaspora

entries.label: Study in the Ḥaramayn
entries.loc: Mecca and Medina · and back to Najd
entries.hint: Najdi scholars went to Mecca and Medina to study and returned with books, licences and connections — the channel that brought Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb his teachers and his sources, and that also carried news of Najd out to the wider Muslim world.
entries.note: Voll on the Medina network; Cook (1992).

entries.label: Basra and the expulsion
entries.hint: Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's time in Basra, where he preached against local shrine practice and was driven out of the city, is the first recorded clash between his doctrine and an established urban Muslim society — a preview of every conflict that followed.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām; the biographical tradition; Cook (1992).

entries.label: The al-Aḥsāʾ connection
entries.hint: The town emirates managed their relations with al-Aḥsāʾ constantly — tribute, appeals for arbitration, marriage, refuge. It was a Banū Khālid threat from al-Aḥsāʾ that expelled the shaykh from al-ʿUyayna and, unintentionally, sent him to Dirʿiyya.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; Ibn Ghannām; al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: The ʿUqaylāt networks abroad
entries.hint: The Qaṣīmi merchant houses kept agents and quarters in the trading cities of Iraq, Syria and Egypt — a Najdi commercial diaspora that tied the poorest interior in Arabia to the region's markets, and later reached Bombay.
entries.note: the ʿUqaylāt trade literature; the later Najdi merchant-family histories.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A stateless, feuding, folk-religious plateau on the eve of a religious revolution that was, in its urgency and its targets, entirely local

entries.label: Stateless Najd on the eve of the reform
entries.hint: A plateau of feuding oasis towns under a distant Banū Khālid overlordship, its folk religion flourishing, its poets recording the disorder — the society the Wahhābī chroniclers would portray as a new jāhiliyya, and that a revolution was about to remake.
entries.note: al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002), which argues the pre-reform picture is partly polemical but the fragmentation real.

entries.label: The reform as a Najdi phenomenon
entries.hint: Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's movement drew on the wider Ḥanbalī hadith revival, but its urgency, its targets — the specific trees and tombs of Najd — and its politics were local. It was a response to the condition of 18th-century Najd, not an import.
entries.note: Cook (1992); DeLong-Bas (2004); al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: The thread continues — the pact and the first Saudi state
entries.hint: The folio ends with the 1744 oath at Dirʿiyya. Within sixty years the alliance of the Āl Saʿūd and the Āl al-Shaykh will have conquered most of the Arabian Peninsula and sacked the shrine cities of Iraq — the subject of the next folio.
entries.note: a forward reference: najd-1744-1900 (the First and Second Saudi Emirates, the Egyptian destruction and the Rashīdī rivalry) is planned but not yet built.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The stoning at al-ʿUyayna, the mostly silent women of the emirate towns, and the enslaved and freed of the oases

entries.label: The woman stoned at al-ʿUyayna
entries.hint: An early and much-cited act of the reform in power: a woman who confessed repeatedly to adultery was stoned on Ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb's judgement — an assertion of the ḥudūd penalties that the town emirates had largely let lapse, and a signal of what the doctrine meant in practice.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar; Cook (1992).

entries.label: Women in the emirate town
entries.hint: Closely secluded in the amīr and merchant households, more visible among the poor and the bedouin. The wedding songs, the laments and the satirical verse attributed to women are most of what survives of their voice from this period.
entries.note: Sowayan on women's Nabaṭī poetry; al-Juhany (2002) on Najdi town society.

entries.label: The enslaved and the freed in the towns
entries.hint: The Gulf slave trade brought enslaved Africans into the Najdi towns as farm and household labour; freedmen — the khadam — formed a recognised low stratum. The reform movement's armies would soon include both enslaved and freed soldiers.
entries.note: Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery' (2006); the Najdi town social structure in al-Juhany (2002).
